blocks.text: The chapter presents Hosea’s action in the first person: he acquires an unnamed woman, establishes a period in which she is to live without other sexual relationships, and then compares that period with Israel’s coming deprivation of political leadership and cultic practice. Important details remain uncertain. The text does not identify the woman as Gomer, though that identification is plausible, and the payment does not by itself prove that this was a purchase, bride-price, debt release, prostitution, or enslavement. Readers also differ over whether the marriage account is biography, symbolic action, literary fiction, or a composition with more than one layer.

sections.title: Questions about the woman and the payment

blocks.text: The marriage imagery in Hosea 3 must not be used to tell a person to remain with an abuser or to justify coercive marriage, sexual humiliation, surveillance, deprivation, or forced reconciliation. Any pastoral use of this passage must center survivor safety, consent, trauma-informed care, and accountability.
